Wei Zhang, Ming Li, Sara Novak, Daniel Kim - Institute of Document Engineering, 1 Science Park Road, 100190

Scientific document ingestion is the bottleneck of retrieval-augmented question answering over research literature. Born-digital PDFs still lose line structure, mix captions into body text, and flatten tables into unreadable streams. In this work we present a controlled benchmark that separates parser errors from chunker errors, and we introduce an element-level schema that makes reading order, furniture, captions, tables and equations comparable across five ingestion pipelines. Our experiments on twelve paper templates show that native text extraction remains the most reliable route for born-digital PDFs, while conditional page-level OCR is required only for scanned pages.
1 Introduction

Retrieval-augmented generation over scientific literature depends on the quality of the ingested corpus. When a PDF is converted into fixed-size token windows, the retrieval unit no longer corresponds to a knowledge unit: page numbers, running heads, watermarks and broken LaTeX fragments enter the index, while figure captions are diluted into paragraphs that discuss unrelated content. Prior work has shown that ranking metrics degrade whenever these structural artefacts dominate the embedding of a chunk [3].

The contribution of this paper is threefold. First, we define a single schema that all ingestion pipelines must emit, and we show that this schema makes heterogeneous parsers directly comparable. Second, we build a controlled template corpus with element-level ground truth so that text fidelity, reading order and table structure can be measured without relying on any parser as a reference. Third, we evaluate conditional OCR strategies and report when native text extraction should be preferred [12], [7].
2 Related Work

Document understanding pipelines such as MinerU, Docling and Marker combine layout detection with structured serialization. These systems recover section hierarchy, tables and formulas, but they differ substantially in their treatment of furniture and in whether they require an external vision-language model [5], [9].

Chunking strategies have evolved from fixed token windows to structure-aware and parent-child schemes. Earlier work in this project showed that element-aware chunking isolates captions and therefore repairs caption dilution failures, at the cost of a much larger number of small retrieval units [2].
3 Method

We model a document as an ordered sequence of typed elements. Each element carries a reading order, a page index, a bounding box and a section path. Let the page width be W and the gutter be G; an element is assigned to the left column whenever its box centre c_x satisfies c_x < (W - G) / 2 [4].
(1) Parse the PDF into raw blocks with explicit bounding boxes.
(2) Normalize Unicode and repair hyphenated line breaks conservatively.
(3) Emit typed elements and drop page furniture from the embedding corpus.
3.1 Encoder

The encoder consumes the concatenated element text and produces a dense representation. Each element is embedded separately so that a caption is never averaged together with the paragraph that follows it [6].
L_enc = - sum_i log P( e_i | e_less_i )      (1)
This objective encourages the encoder to model element boundaries rather than surface fluency, which is what retrieval actually needs.
3.2 Decoder
The decoder reconstructs a compact document representation that preserves section boundaries. Long tables are split row-wise and the header row is repeated in every part.
H = LayerNorm( x + MultiHead( x, x, x ) )      (2)
Figure 1: Overview of the proposed ingestion pipeline. Raw PDF pages are converted into typed elements, cleaned of page furniture, and chunked along section and element boundaries.
Figure 1 summarizes the pipeline. The parser produces typed elements, the cleaner removes page furniture, and the chunker merges sibling paragraphs while isolating captions and tables [8].
4 Experiments

We evaluate five ingestion pipelines on twelve templates and on a real corpus of ten point-cloud completion papers. All retrieval experiments use the same dense encoder, the same query set and the same candidate depth so that only ingestion changes [10].
4.1 Dataset

The controlled corpus contains one logical document rendered under twelve templates with identical textual content. Every element is annotated with its type, section path and reading order, which makes parser errors attributable to a specific page and box.

Method CD F1 PCN 8.20 0.855 PoinTr 7.83 0.871 AdaPoinTr 7.41 0.885 Ours 7.05 0.901
4.2 Ablation
Table 2 isolates the contribution of each loss term. Removing the consistency loss costs 0.6 CD points, which confirms that structural supervision is not redundant.
L_total = L_cd + lambda_1 L_rec + lambda_2 L_con      (3)
Table 2: Ablation on the decoding head. The first row spans all columns.

Figure 2 shows that qualitative gains are consistent with the quantitative table. We attribute the improvement to the geometry-aware attention introduced in Section 3.2.
5 Conclusion

We presented a schema-first benchmark for scientific document ingestion. The controlled corpus turns an otherwise subjective question into a measurable one, and it shows that structure-preserving ingestion is a prerequisite for retrieval quality [1].
